paragraphs: Haussler’s convolution kernel compares structured objects by breaking them into components, comparing every possible pair of components, and adding the results. If the component comparison is a positive semidefinite kernel, this construction preserves that property. The paper asks what happens when only a selected subset of component pairs contributes to the comparison.

The proposed mapping kernel makes precisely this generalization. Selecting pairs creates more flexibility, but positive semidefiniteness no longer follows simply from the original construction. The paper provides and proves an easily checkable necessary and sufficient condition for mapping kernels. This replaces separate analyses of individual examples, some of which had previously reached incorrect conclusions.

The authors also introduce kernels based on distributions of index-structure sizes and edit costs. These extend ideas behind measures such as maximum agreement trees and edit distance by considering distributional information rather than only an extreme value. Improved performance is presented as a reasonable expectation, while the established contribution is the general validity condition and the new constructions.
icml-2008-a-generalization-of-haussler-s.tldr: Mapping kernels generalize convolution kernels to selected component pairs, with a proven condition determining positive semidefiniteness.

paragraphs: Training a structured predictor requires comparing a correct output with competing outputs that may contain many linked decisions. Two maximum-margin approaches, margin scaling and slack scaling, handle these comparisons differently. Margin scaling is widely used because its inference resembles ordinary structured prediction; slack scaling is regarded as more accurate and better behaved, but has an inference bottleneck.

The paper first develops an efficient variational approximation to slack scaling that addresses this bottleneck while retaining its reported accuracy advantage. It then raises a separate concern: existing approaches may generate competing outputs without comprehensively separating the correct labeling. The proposed PosLearn trainer generates violations that enforce separation at each position when the loss decomposes across positions.

Experiments on real datasets show test-error reductions of up to 25% with PosLearn. Its competing outputs can also be generated more efficiently than slack-scaling violations; for many structured tasks, the required time is twice that of MAP inference. These findings connect the choice of training constraints to both prediction accuracy and computational effort.
icml-2008-accurate-max-margin-training-f.tldr: The paper makes slack scaling more tractable and introduces PosLearn, whose positionwise training constraints improve accuracy and efficiency in reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a Bayesian approach to multiple instance learning that combines classifier training with automatic feature selection. Instead of treating every available feature as equally useful throughout learning, the method identifies a relevant subset. Feature selection is therefore part of the learning algorithm, connecting the classifier it produces with a smaller collection of useful inputs.

The approach also supports learning several conceptually related classifiers through inductive transfer. In this setting, information from related learning tasks can help train an individual classifier. The paper treats this sharing as an additional capability of the Bayesian method, alongside its baseline ability to learn a classifier and identify relevant features.

The reported experiments distinguish the benefits of these two elements. The baseline method achieves higher accuracy than previous multiple instance learning algorithms while selecting substantially fewer useful features. Adding inductive transfer further improves accuracy compared with training each task separately. Together, these results support combining feature selection and learning across related tasks in the evaluated problems.
icml-2008-bayesian-multiple-instance-lea.tldr: A Bayesian multiple instance learning method selects fewer useful features and improves reported accuracy, with further gains from transferring information across related tasks.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix models support collaborative filtering by representing a large collection of ratings through a more compact set of parameters. A common training approach finds a single maximum a posteriori, or MAP, estimate. Although computationally efficient even on large datasets, this approach can overfit unless its regularization parameters are chosen carefully.

The paper gives probabilistic matrix factorization a fully Bayesian treatment. It integrates over model parameters and hyperparameters, allowing model capacity to be controlled automatically through this treatment of uncertainty. Markov chain Monte Carlo supplies the computational method for training the Bayesian model, making the integration-based approach usable on a substantial ratings dataset.

The authors demonstrate the method on the Netflix dataset, containing more than 100 million user–movie ratings. Their Bayesian models achieve significantly higher prediction accuracy than probabilistic matrix factorization trained with MAP estimation. The result supports the practical value of accounting for parameter uncertainty and shows that this fuller Bayesian treatment can be trained efficiently at the reported scale.
icml-2008-bayesian-probabilistic-matrix-.tldr: Bayesian matrix factorization integrates over parameters and hyperparameters, improving Netflix rating predictions over MAP-trained models in the reported study.

paragraphs: Quantile regression predicts a chosen point in a conditional distribution, so changing the requested quantile changes the predictive modeling problem. Its loss function explicitly depends on that choice. With regularized kernel quantile regression and cross-validation, finding models across quantiles therefore produces a family of related optimization problems.

The paper shows how to follow the path of cross-validated solutions as the quantile parameter changes. Each individual problem has a non-convex, bi-level structure, making direct optimization challenging. Nevertheless, the authors prove that the way the optimal cross-validated solution evolves permits it to be tracked. The key opportunity lies in the relationship among solutions at different quantiles.

They turn this property into an algorithm and demonstrate it on data. Following the solution path allows efficient treatment of the entire family of bi-level problems. The contribution is thus more than fitting a model for one requested quantile: it provides a proven way to organize the computation across varying quantiles while retaining cross-validation within the problem.
icml-2008-bi-level-path-following-for-cr.tldr: A proven path-following method efficiently tracks cross-validated kernel quantile regression solutions as the requested quantile changes.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning from high-dimensional data by combining the search for a compact representation with the training of a predictor. Its supervised dimensionality reduction framework places feature extraction and prediction inside one optimization problem. This makes the representation part of the predictive learning task, so the two components are learned together.

The framework uses generalized linear models chosen to suit the data and prediction target. It covers both classification and regression, giving a family of algorithms rather than a method tied to just one kind of output. The unifying idea is to coordinate dimensionality reduction with the statistical model used for prediction.

The algorithms have simple closed-form update rules and a proof of convergence. Closed-form updates describe how individual optimization steps are computed; the convergence result addresses the behavior of the overall procedure. Experiments on several high-dimensional datasets provide promising empirical results. Together, the stated contributions combine a unified learning formulation, manageable updates, and theoretical support for the optimization process.
icml-2008-closed-form-supervised-dimensi.tldr: The paper jointly learns compact representations and GLM predictors using closed-form updates with a convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: This paper connects compressed sensing with Bayesian experimental design: choosing measurements becomes part of the inference problem. It develops an efficient approximate design method based on expectation propagation. The method learns measurement filters for full images, bringing the choice of what to measure into the modeling framework.

A large comparison of linear measurements of natural images yields a striking empirical ordering. Measuring wavelet coefficients in a simple top-down sequence systematically outperforms the tested compressed sensing methods using random measurements. A previously proposed sequential projection optimization approach performs still worse. The authors’ approximate Bayesian method learns filters that outperform the wavelet heuristic in this study.

These findings show that measurement design can materially affect results on the examined image problems. The framework also accommodates notions of signal complexity beyond sparsity and can use other noise models. The authors present ideas for scaling to larger signal representations, while their demonstrated contribution is efficient learning of useful measurement filters for images of realistic size.
icml-2008-compressed-sensing-and-bayesia.tldr: An approximate Bayesian measurement-design method learns image filters that outperform both tested random compressed sensing measurements and a strong wavelet heuristic.

paragraphs: The paper develops a spectral approach to estimating mixture distributions, focusing on Gaussian mixtures. Its guiding analogy is spectroscopy: the interaction between a probe and a substance reveals something about the substance. Here, a kernel function acts as the probe, and the observed data supply the material being examined.

Computationally, the relevant spectrum consists of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a kernel matrix constructed from the samples. The authors show how this information can reveal aspects of the underlying distribution. Their framework extends ideas and analyses associated with spectral clustering and kernel principal component analysis toward estimating the parameters of a probabilistic mixture.

The resulting algorithms estimate the number of Gaussian components as well as their means and covariance matrices. This makes the spectral information useful for describing both the mixture’s structure and its individual components. The paper supplies a theoretical framework and encouraging experimental results, supporting spectral analysis as a route to distribution estimation in the studied setting.
icml-2008-data-spectroscopy-learning-mix.tldr: Data spectroscopy uses kernel-matrix eigenstructure to estimate Gaussian mixture components, including their number, means, and covariances.

paragraphs: The learning problem starts with groups of observations whose individual labels are unknown. What is available for each group is the proportion belonging to each label. The goal is to predict individual labels for another group, whose label proportions are also known. Supervision therefore comes from group summaries rather than directly labeled examples.

The paper introduces consistent estimators for recovering labels from this information. It establishes that correct labels can be reconstructed with high probability in a uniform convergence sense. This is a probabilistic theoretical claim about the estimators’ behavior, giving the approach support beyond an observation that aggregate proportions sometimes seem useful.

Experiments indicate that the method also works well in practice. The abstract identifies e-commerce, spam filtering, and improper content detection as settings where the problem arises. The central contribution is a way to connect information about label frequencies across groups to predictions for individual observations, with both a stated convergence result and empirical evidence supporting that connection.
icml-2008-estimating-labels-from-label-p.tldr: The paper learns individual labels from known group label proportions, with high-probability reconstruction results and positive experimental evidence.

paragraphs: The paper studies a constrained version of finding the dominant eigenvector of a sample covariance matrix, a central operation in principal component analysis. One constraint limits how many vector entries may be nonzero. Another imposes non-negativity, keeping the entries aligned in sign. These restrictions connect the extracted component with feature selection and dimensionality reduction.

The authors derive an algorithm from expectation-maximization for probabilistic PCA. It handles either constraint individually or both together, providing a common approach to sparse and non-negative variants. The sparsity constraint controls how many original dimensions contribute, while non-negativity restricts the form of their contributions.

The stated computational complexity grows at most quadratically with the number of data dimensions. Experiments on large datasets from biology and computer vision show significant improvements in performance and computational efficiency relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines flexibility in the allowed constraints with evidence that the resulting optimization method is useful on substantial datasets.
icml-2008-expectation-maximization-for-s.tldr: An expectation-maximization algorithm handles sparse and non-negative PCA constraints with at most quadratic complexity in data dimensionality.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to rank nearby or related nodes in a large graph using proximity measures based on random walks. It combines an existing deterministic pruning algorithm with sampling, producing approximately correct rankings with high probability at query time. This makes the ranking computation responsive to the current query.

A second contribution explains locality properties of these proximity measures through the short-term behavior of random walks. These theoretical results accompany an algorithm that can answer queries without caching information about the entire graph. The combination matters because the method addresses both how to search efficiently and why the chosen proximity measures have useful local behavior.

On a Citeseer author–word–citation graph with 600,000 nodes, the reported average query time is about four seconds on a single-CPU machine. The authors also evaluate link prediction tasks, outperforming Personalized PageRank on most of them. These results provide evidence for practical query speed and prediction quality in the evaluated graph setting.
icml-2008-fast-incremental-proximity-sea.tldr: Combining pruning and sampling enables fast, approximately correct graph proximity rankings, supported by locality results and link-prediction experiments.

paragraphs: The paper formulates a structure-design problem for hidden Markov models and stochastic context-free grammars. Motivated by protein and RNA design, it reverses the perspective of familiar decoding algorithms such as Viterbi and CKY. The objective is to use these probabilistic formalisms for design, prompting a new algorithmic question about the inverse problem.

The authors establish a strong computational hardness result: the problem is NP-complete even when the emission alphabet contains only three letters. Their proof uses a reduction from 3-SAT and has implications for the difficulty of RNA secondary structure design. Thus, a small alphabet alone does not remove the general computational obstacle.

They then develop approaches to tractability. For hidden Markov models, a branch-and-bound algorithm has fixed-parameter tractable worst-case running time: exponential in the number of model states but linear in structure length. They also formulate the problem as a mixed integer linear program. These results identify both the general difficulty and concrete ways to organize its computation.
icml-2008-inverting-the-viterbi-algorith.tldr: The paper formalizes inverse decoding for structure design, proves NP-completeness, and develops parameterized and mixed-integer optimization approaches.

paragraphs: A document can be relevant on its own while adding little to a ranking already filled with similar results. The paper argues that treating relevance as independent across documents can therefore produce redundancy. It develops two algorithms that learn diverse rankings directly from users’ clicking behavior, motivated by users’ preference for variety near the top.

The algorithms target reduced abandonment or, alternatively, a higher probability of finding a relevant document among the first k positions. This frames ranking quality around what the collection of highly placed documents provides to a user. Click behavior supplies the feedback used to learn that collection.

The two algorithms have different strengths. One asymptotically reaches the best payoff achievable in polynomial time even when user interests change. The other performs better empirically when interests remain static and has a near-optimality guarantee in that setting. The results distinguish adaptation to changing interests from stronger observed performance under stable interests, while preserving diversity as the common objective.
icml-2008-learning-diverse-rankings-with.tldr: Two click-driven ranking algorithms learn diversity, with different theoretical and empirical strengths for changing versus static user interests.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable configuration of a Markov random field can be approached through a linear programming relaxation. The paper focuses on the first-order tree-based relaxation and addresses a gap in existing algorithms: the previously discussed methods lacked a guarantee of solving that LP for every problem.

The proposed family of solvers uses proximal minimization with Bregman divergences while exploiting the graph’s structure. Each algorithm has two loops. The outer loop advances the proximal optimization sequence; the inner loop computes an update through cyclic Bregman operations. Because these inner updates are distributed according to the graph, they can be implemented as message passing.

The authors establish convergence guarantees and illustrate performance on medium and large problems. They also introduce tree-based rounding with provable optimality guarantees, addressing the step from a relaxed solution toward a structured assignment. The central contribution is to connect graph-respecting computation with reliable LP optimization, alongside a theoretically supported rounding procedure.
icml-2008-message-passing-for-graph-stru.tldr: Graph-structured proximal algorithms provide provably convergent message-passing LP solvers, accompanied by a tree-based rounding scheme with optimality guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper addresses population-structure inference when genetic variation reflects both population mixing and mutations. Traditional approaches such as Structure omit mutational effects. The proposed mStruct model brings mutation estimation into the same analysis as population structure, allowing both processes to contribute to the explanation of the observed genetic data.

Its hierarchical Bayesian formulation represents admixture through population-specific mixtures of inheritance models. A variational algorithm performs inference in this framework. This construction provides a shared model for estimating population relationships and mutation patterns, making mutation-related outputs part of the analysis rather than leaving them outside the representation.

The authors validate mStruct on synthetic data and apply it to HGDP microsatellite and SNP datasets. They compare its inferred maps of world population structure with those from Structure. They also report potentially interesting mutation patterns that Structure cannot estimate. The stated findings demonstrate the model’s additional analytical capability, while treating the biological interest of the inferred mutation patterns as provisional.
icml-2008-mstruct-a-new-admixture-model-.tldr: mStruct jointly models population admixture and mutation, producing population-structure estimates and potentially informative mutation patterns.

paragraphs: The paper studies multiclass prediction from categorical features using grid clustering. Each feature’s possible values are partitioned into groups, and combining those partitions creates a grid over the full parameter space. A classifier built on this organization depends on how the categorical values have been grouped.

The authors derive a generalization bound for these classification schemes. The bound evaluates clustering solutions through the predictive generalization of the classifier built from them. For classification using a single feature, it can be used to find a globally optimal classification rule. This gives the bound a constructive role as well as an evaluative one.

The single-feature analysis also supports feature ranking: features can be compared according to their resulting generalization power. In the reported experiments, this use of the bound is much more precise than rankings based on mutual information or normalized correlation indices. The contribution connects categorical clustering, classifier construction, and feature evaluation through one theoretically motivated criterion.
icml-2008-multi-classification-by-catego.tldr: A generalization bound evaluates categorical grid classifiers and supports single-feature optimization and empirically more precise feature ranking.

paragraphs: Compressive sensing can reduce the measurements needed to recover a signal when appropriate conditions hold. This paper considers applications involving several signals, each associated with its own sensing task. The central question is how to reconstruct those signals while also deciding what information should be shared across their tasks.

The authors propose a Bayesian framework with a Dirichlet process prior. This prior supplies a principled mechanism for inferring the sharing relationships at the same time as performing each task’s compressive sensing inversion. The sharing arrangement is therefore itself part of the inference problem, connecting decisions about relationships among tasks with the recovery of their signals.

A variational Bayesian algorithm estimates the posterior distribution over the model parameters. This treatment represents uncertainty across the modeled quantities while fitting the coupled tasks. The main contribution is the unified formulation: signal reconstruction and the determination of appropriate sharing are handled together, providing a framework for multiple sensing problems whose relationships need to be inferred.
icml-2008-multi-task-compressive-sensing.tldr: A Bayesian compressive sensing framework jointly reconstructs multiple signals and infers how their sensing tasks should share information.

paragraphs: Deep belief networks are generative models with multiple layers of hidden variables, built using restricted Boltzmann machines. Their practical training methods had enabled successful applications, but quantitative evaluation remained difficult. A key obstacle is the partition function in an RBM, which makes exact likelihood learning, model selection, and complexity control intractable.

Annealed importance sampling can efficiently estimate this partition function. The paper introduces an AIS scheme for comparing RBMs with different architectures. This provides a quantitative route to assessing architectural choices through the probabilistic models themselves, despite the difficulty of calculating the required normalization exactly.

For deeper belief networks, the authors combine an AIS estimator with approximate inference to estimate a lower bound on test-data log-probability. The distinction matters: the evaluated quantity is an estimated bound, rather than an exact probability calculation. The authors position this as an initial step toward directly measuring how well deep belief networks serve as generative models of data.
icml-2008-on-the-quantitative-analysis-o.tldr: Annealed importance sampling enables quantitative RBM comparisons and estimation of a test-data log-probability lower bound for deep belief networks.

paragraphs: Kernel-based Bayesian reinforcement learning methods such as Gaussian Process Temporal Difference represent uncertainty in value functions and allow prior knowledge to be specified. Their empirical performance, however, depends strongly on the chosen prior. The paper addresses selecting this model online, as the learning process proceeds.

The proposed Replacing-Kernel RL method uses population-based search to perform online model selection for GPTD. Kernel selection matters because the kernel expresses prior covariance between states: it determines how the model initially relates their values. Searching over kernels gives the agent a way to obtain useful relationships that may be difficult to specify manually.

The authors compare the method with standard GPTD and tile-coding across several reinforcement learning domains. They report significantly better asymptotic performance for many kernel families. The resulting kernels also express an intuitively useful notion of state covariance. These findings support online prior selection as a practical contributor to the performance of the evaluated Bayesian learning agents.
icml-2008-online-kernel-selection-for-ba.tldr: Replacing-Kernel RL searches for GPTD kernels online, improving reported asymptotic performance and learning useful relationships between states.

paragraphs: Distributed reinforcement learning involves agents learning control policies through interactions with environments. Earlier work emphasized obtaining useful policies while limiting how much agents share about their experiences. This paper adds a stronger requirement: states, rewards, and actions may contain confidential information that agents want to keep private.

Limiting communication alone does not provide a theoretical privacy guarantee. The authors therefore formulate privacy preservation as an explicit part of the distributed learning problem. This shifts attention to whether the necessary joint learning computations can be performed without requiring agents to disclose their private information to one another.

Their solutions use secure function evaluation, a cryptographic primitive for computing with private inputs. In standard reinforcement learning settings, the proposed constructions achieve optimal policies without requiring the agents to share those private inputs. The contribution connects the learning objective with a cryptographic mechanism, showing how policy optimization and the stated privacy requirement can be addressed together in the considered settings.
icml-2008-privacy-preserving-reinforceme.tldr: Secure function evaluation allows distributed agents to learn optimal policies in standard settings without sharing their private states, rewards, or actions.

paragraphs: Object recognition often represents an object through a collection of local features, such as interest points or regions. These collections can vary in size and lack a fixed ordering, complicating kernel design. The paper develops a context-dependent kernel that accounts for both feature matching and the geometric relationships among features.

Matching is expressed through an energy function with three ingredients. A fidelity term measures the quality of feature correspondences, a neighborhood term captures object geometry, and a regularization term completes the objective. This construction allows the surrounding arrangement of features to influence the resulting comparison between objects.

The authors show that the energy’s fixed point defines a context-dependent kernel satisfying the Mercer condition, establishing its suitability for kernel methods. In object-recognition experiments, SVMs using this kernel clearly outperform SVMs using context-free kernels. The results support incorporating geometric context into object comparisons, while the theoretical result connects the matching construction to a valid kernel.
icml-2008-robust-matching-and-recognitio.tldr: A valid context-dependent kernel combines local feature similarity with object geometry and improves SVM recognition in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Representing documents as word-count vectors is straightforward, but it poorly captures relationships between similar words and ambiguities in word meaning. This paper uses deep networks to learn compact document representations for retrieval and classification. The aim is to retain informative properties of a document within a much smaller representation.

Training combines an unsupervised objective with a supervised objective. This lets the representation learning process use both document information and available labels. The authors report that even a small number of labeled examples is very advantageous during training, making the supervised component useful when labels are limited.

Experiments compare favorably with related methods that produce sparse and binary representations. The paper also shows that deep, nonlinear models can produce extremely compact representations efficiently. Together, these findings support learning document encodings through combined objectives: the representation can be small while remaining informative, and limited supervision can improve the learning process in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2008-semi-supervised-learning-of-co.tldr: Deep networks trained with supervised and unsupervised objectives learn compact document representations, benefiting substantially from even a few labeled examples.

paragraphs: The paper examines an unusual relationship between dataset size and the time required to optimize a support vector machine. Its central argument is that optimization runtime should decrease as the training set grows. The quantity under discussion is the runtime of the optimization procedure, making the relationship between data volume and computational effort the main subject.

The authors investigate a simple subgradient descent approach and provide both theoretical and empirical results showing this behavior. Subgradient descent is the specific optimization method supporting their claim. The contribution therefore includes an analysis of the proposed runtime relationship and observations that demonstrate it for the studied approach.

The stated scope is at least the case of linear kernels. Within that scope, the results give a concrete example in which more training data accompanies less optimization time. The paper’s significance lies in this counterintuitive computational finding and its support from both analysis and experiments, with the kernel qualification remaining part of the claim.
icml-2008-svm-optimization-inverse-depen.tldr: Theoretical and empirical results show that simple subgradient SVM optimization can become faster as training data increases, at least for linear kernels.

paragraphs: The dynamic hierarchical Dirichlet process models sequential datasets whose statistical properties change over time. At each time point, the observations receive a mixture representation within the hierarchical Dirichlet process framework. This provides a way to describe the data at individual times while also modeling relationships across the sequence.

Consecutive time points are connected through a random parameter controlling their probabilistic similarity. The connection allows the model to represent temporal relationships alongside the mixture description at each time. The authors derive the mechanisms through which the evolving data share information, making temporal sharing an explicit part of the probabilistic formulation.

The paper also develops a relatively simple Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler for inference and presents experiments demonstrating the model. Its contribution combines a model of changing distributions with a computational procedure for working with that model. The important structural idea is that neighboring time points are related through a probabilistic similarity parameter while retaining their own mixture representations.
icml-2008-the-dynamic-hierarchical-diric.tldr: The dynamic hierarchical Dirichlet process links time-specific mixture models through a random parameter governing similarity between consecutive datasets.

paragraphs: GroupLASSO identifies important explanatory factors organized into groups, but its solutions can be ambiguous and expensive to compute. Ambiguity matters when interpreting which groups are selected: a reported solution may not be unique. This paper addresses both the mathematical uniqueness question and the computational burden of large problems.

The authors formulate conditions for uniqueness that yield an easily implemented testing procedure. The test also identifies all groups that could potentially be active. This gives information beyond a single fitted solution, helping expose ambiguity in which explanatory groups the method may select.

These results support an efficient algorithm capable of handling input dimensions in the millions and efficiently approximating the solution path. Applications to large-scale learning problems exhibit excellent reported performance. The authors also show that the test helps prevent misinterpretations of GroupLASSO results. The contribution connects reliable interpretation with scalable computation by using information about possible solutions to guide both.
icml-2008-the-group-lasso-for-generalize.tldr: A GroupLASSO uniqueness test identifies potentially active groups and supports efficient optimization with millions of input dimensions.
